label: lem:AF-conditioning
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $\tau_\ell=\inf\{s:A_s>\ell\}$, with $\inf\emptyset=\infty$.
		Then $\tau_\ell$ is a stopping time, and the Stieltjes change of variables gives  (see \cite[Proposition~0.4.10]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales})
		\[
		\int_a^b F\circ\theta_s\,dA_s
		=\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\le\tau_\ell<b\}}
		F\circ\theta_{\tau_\ell}\,d\ell.
		\]
		Endpoint and plateau levels have zero Lebesgue measure. Conditioning at
		$\tau_\ell$ and using the strong Markov property gives the bound
		$K\operatorname{E}_y\int_0^\infty\mathbf1_{\{a\le\tau_\ell<b\}}d\ell$, which is
		\eqref{eq:AF-conditioning}. 
		The interchange of expectation and integration is justified by localization in time and level and then applying monotone convergence.
		
		For integer $p\ge2$, continuity and monotonicity give
		\[
		A_t^p=p\int_0^t(A_t-A_s)^{p-1}\,dA_s.
		\]
		Since $A_t-A_s=A_{t-s}\circ\theta_s\le A_t\circ\theta_s$, induction and \eqref{eq:AF-conditioning} give
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_y A_t^p\le p(p-1)!M(t)^{p-1}\operatorname{E}_y A_t\le p!M(t)^p.
		\]
		All integrals are nonnegative, so Tonelli and truncation justify the induction
		without any prior moment assumption. Applying the same argument after time
		$u$ gives the increment estimate for integer powers; Lyapunov's inequality
		with $p=\lceil q\rceil$ gives the real exponents. 
		This is the standard ordered-integral (Kac moment) argument for positive continuous additive functionals; see \cite[Section~3.1]{fitzsimmons1999kac}.
		The same Kac moment machinery also yields the two-point local-time moment identity used in Example~\ref{ex:abstract-benchmarks}.

label: eq:abstract-covariance
title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: mixing and discounted potentials.} 
		Since \(S\) is finite and the chain is irreducible, the transition
		semigroup \(P_t^\alpha=e^{tQ}\) is exponentially ergodic: there exist
		constants \(C,c>0\) such that
		\[
		\sup_{i,j\in S}
		\left|P_{ij}^\alpha(t)-\pi_j\right|
		\le Ce^{-ct},
		\qquad t\ge0;
		\]
		see, e.g., \cite[Section~6.6]{anderson1991_book}. For bounded \(h\),
		with
		\[
		\widetilde h:=h-\pi(h),
		\qquad
		\pi(\widetilde h)=0,
		\]
		we have
		\[
		\|P_t^\alpha\widetilde h\|_\infty
		\le C_h e^{-ct},
		\qquad t\ge0,
		\]
		where \(C_h:=|S|C\|\widetilde h\|_\infty\). Therefore, for \(r\le s\),
		the Markov property gives
		\begin{align}\label{eq:abstract-covariance}
			\left|\operatorname{E}_i^\alpha[\widetilde h(\alpha_{r/\varepsilon})
			\widetilde h(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})]\right|
			&=\left|\operatorname{E}_i^\alpha[\widetilde h(\alpha_{r/\varepsilon})
			(P^\alpha_{(s-r)/\varepsilon}\widetilde h)(\alpha_{r/\varepsilon})]\right|\notag\\
			&\le C_he^{-c(s-r)/\varepsilon}.
		\end{align}
		No stationarity is used here. Integrating by parts against $\operatorname{E}_yA_s$ gives
		\begin{align}\label{eq:abstract-weighted-potential}
			U_\varepsilon(T):=\sup_y\operatorname{E}_y\int_0^T e^{-cs/\varepsilon}\,dA_s
			&\le e^{-cT/\varepsilon}M(T)
			+\frac c\varepsilon\int_0^T e^{-cs/\varepsilon}M(s)\,ds\notag\\
			&\le C_T\varepsilon^\vartheta.
		\end{align}
		
		\medskip\noindent\emph{Step 2: interval and random-time estimates.}
		Lemma~\ref{lem:AF-conditioning} gives the integrability needed for Fubini.
		Condition on the base path. Since \(\tau\) is measurable with respect to
		that path, both \(A\) and \(\tau\) are then fixed. Since \(A\) is continuous,
		its Stieltjes measure \(dA\) is atomless, so the diagonal has zero
		\(dA\otimes dA\)-measure.
		Therefore,
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{y,i}|J_\varepsilon(\tau)|^2
		\le 2C_h\operatorname{E}_y\int_0^T\int_s^T
		e^{-c(r-s)/\varepsilon}\,dA_r\,dA_s
		\le 2C_h U_\varepsilon(T)\operatorname{E}_y A_T,
		\]
		where \eqref{eq:AF-conditioning} is applied to
		$F=\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\,dA_u$ after enlarging the remaining
		future horizon to $T$. 
		Together with
		\eqref{eq:abstract-weighted-potential} and
		our assumption \eqref{eq:abstract-A-first}, this proves
		\eqref{eq:abstract-random-time}.
		
		The same calculation on a deterministic interval \([a,b]\) yields
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-interval}
			\operatorname{E}_{y,i}|J_\varepsilon(b)-J_\varepsilon(a)|^2
			\le
			C_{T,h}\varepsilon^\vartheta
			\operatorname{E}_y(A_b-A_a),
			\qquad 0\le a\le b\le T.
		\end{equation}
		The dependence on the interval through the increment \(A_b-A_a\) will be
		important below. Indeed, if
		\[
		0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T
		\]
		is any deterministic partition of \([0,T]\), then
		\[
		\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}
		\operatorname{E}_y\!\left(A_{t_{k+1}}-A_{t_k}\right)
		=
		\operatorname{E}_y A_T.
		\]
		Thus, summing \eqref{eq:abstract-interval} over all intervals at one dyadic
		level introduces no factor proportional to the number of intervals.
		
		\medskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: dyadic maximal bound.}
		Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let
		\[
		G_m=\{kT2^{-m}:0\le k\le2^m\}
		\]
		be the dyadic grid of mesh size \(T2^{-m}\) on \([0,T]\), and for
		\(0\le j\le m\) and \(0\le k<2^j\), define
		\[
		D_{j,k}
		:=
		J_\varepsilon((k+1)T2^{-j})
		-
		J_\varepsilon(kT2^{-j}),
		\]
		the increment of \(J_\varepsilon\) over the \(k\)-th dyadic interval at
		level \(j\).
		Every interval \([0,t]\), with \(t\in G_m\), admits a dyadic decomposition
		into disjoint intervals, containing at most one interval from each level
		\(0\le j\le m\). Hence the corresponding telescoping decomposition of
		\(J_\varepsilon(t)\) yields
		\[
		\max_{t\in G_m}|J_\varepsilon(t)|
		\le\sum_{j=0}^m\max_{k<2^j}|D_{j,k}|.
		\]
		At each level the intervals partition $[0,T]$, and \eqref{eq:abstract-interval} implies
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{y,i}\max_{k<2^j}|D_{j,k}|^2
		\le\sum_{k<2^j}\operatorname{E}_{y,i}|D_{j,k}|^2
		\le C_{T,h}\varepsilon^\vartheta\operatorname{E}_y A_T.
		\]
		Therefore, by \eqref{eq:abstract-A-first} and Minkowski's inequality,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-grid-points}
			\left(\operatorname{E}_{y,i}\max_{t\in G_m}|J_\varepsilon(t)|^2\right)^{1/2}
			\le C_{T,h}(m+1)\varepsilon^{\vartheta/2}.
		\end{equation}
		
		Choose an integer $p>\max\{2,1/\vartheta\}$ and set $\delta:=T2^{-m}$. Between grid points,
		\[
		|J_\varepsilon(t)-J_\varepsilon(k\delta)|
		\le\|\widetilde h\|_\infty(A_{(k+1)\delta}-A_{k\delta}).
		\]
		Using \eqref{eq:abstract-A-increments} and concavity of $x^{2/p}$,
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_y\max_{k<2^m}(A_{(k+1)\delta}-A_{k\delta})^2
		\le\left(\sum_{k<2^m}\operatorname{E}_y(A_{(k+1)\delta}-A_{k\delta})^p\right)^{2/p}
		\le C_{T,p}\delta^{2\vartheta-2/p}.
		\]
		Consequently,
		\begin{equation}\label{eq:abstract-balance}
			\operatorname{E}_{y,i}\sup_{t\le T}|J_\varepsilon(t)|^2
			\le C_{T,h,p}\big((m+1)^2\varepsilon^\vartheta
			+\delta^{2\vartheta-2/p}\big).
		\end{equation}
		For small $\varepsilon$, choose the dyadic mesh so that
		$\delta\asymp\varepsilon^{\vartheta/(2\vartheta-2/p)}$. Then
		$m= \log_2(T/\delta) =O(1+|\log\varepsilon|)$ and the interpolation term is
		$O(\varepsilon^\vartheta)$. The remaining values of $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$
		are absorbed into the constant using
		$|J_\varepsilon|\le\|\widetilde h\|_\infty A_T$.
		This proves the uniform-in-time bound, and completes the proof.

title: Remark
body_md:
The integrand may also depend on the base process, provided
the switching chain remains independent of it.
Indeed, let \(g:E\times S\to\mathbb R\) be bounded and measurable, and set
\[
\overline g(y):=\sum_{i\in S}\pi_i g(y,i).
\]
Then the same estimates apply to
\[
J_\varepsilon^g(t)
=
\int_0^t
\bigl[g(Y_s,\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline g(Y_s)\bigr]\,dA_s.
\]
Indeed, conditional on the base path, the functions
\[
h_s(i):=g(Y_s,i)-\overline g(Y_s)
\]
are deterministic, centered with respect to \(\pi\), and uniformly bounded by
\(2\|g\|_\infty\). Exponential ergodicity of the chain therefore gives, uniformly
in \(r\le s\),
\[
\left|
\operatorname{E}_i^\alpha
\left[
h_r(\alpha_{r/\varepsilon})
h_s(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})
\right]
\right|
\le
C_g e^{-c(s-r)/\varepsilon}.
\]
The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:abstract-averaging} then applies without change.
Consequently, \eqref{eq:abstract-random-time} and
\eqref{eq:abstract-max} remain valid, with constants depending on
\(\|g\|_\infty\).

label: ex:abstract-benchmarks
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:abstract-benchmarks}
		For bounded nonnegative $V$, $A_t=\int_0^t V(Y_s)\,ds$ satisfies \eqref{eq:abstract-A-first} with $\vartheta=1$. A singular example, without a reflecting boundary, is the symmetric local time $\ell_t^0$ at zero of  standard one-dimensional Brownian motion $B$. 
		With $p_s(x,y)$ its heat kernel,
		\[
		\sup_x\operatorname{E}_x\ell_t^0
		=\sup_x\int_0^t p_s(x,0)\,ds
		=\sqrt{2t/\pi},
		\]
		so the bound~\eqref{eq:abstract-A-first} holds for $\vartheta=1/2$. 
		The identity
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x\ell_t^0=\int_0^t p_s(x,0)\,ds
		\]
		follows from the occupation-density formula
		\cite[Corollary~VI.1.9]
		{revuz1999Continuous_martingales}.
		
		The exponent $\vartheta=1/2$ is attained in the following simple benchmark.
		Let \(B_0=0\) and let \(H\) be an independent sign chain on
		\(S=\{-1,1\}\) with generator and invariant law
		\[
		Q=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			-a & a\\
			a & -a
		\end{pmatrix},
		\qquad
		\pi=
		\left(\frac12,\frac12\right).
		\]
		
		Assume that \(H\) is started from \(\pi\). Then \(H\) is stationary and centered in the sense that \(\operatorname{E}(H_t)=0\) for all \(t\ge 0\), and its covariance formula reads
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:covariance_formula}
			\operatorname{E}[H_sH_r]=e^{-2a|s-r|}.
		\end{equation}
		
		Conditioning on the Brownian path and using the independence of \(H\) and
		\(B\), together with~\eqref{eq:covariance_formula}, gives
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}\left|\int_0^T H_{s/\varepsilon}\,d\ell_s^0\right|^2
			&= \operatorname{E}\left[\int_0^T \int_0^T H_{r/\varepsilon}\,H_{s/\varepsilon}\,d\ell_r^0\,d\ell_s^0\right]
			\\
			&= \operatorname{E}\left[
			\int_0^T\int_0^T
			e^{-2a|s-r|/\varepsilon}\,
			d\ell_r^0\,d\ell_s^0
			\right].
		\end{align}
		For every nonnegative Borel function \(g\), applying the space--time
		occupation-times formula
		\cite[Exercise~VI.1.15]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales}
		to \((s,a)\mapsto g(s)\eta_\delta(a)\), where
		\[
		\eta_\delta(a):=\frac{1}{2\delta}\mathbf 1_{\{|a|<\delta\}},
		\]
		then taking expectations and letting \(\delta\downarrow0\), gives
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x\left[\int_0^t g(s)\,d\ell_s^0\right]
		=
		\int_0^t g(s)p_s(x,0)\,ds.
		\]
		Using this identity together with Tonelli's theorem, the additivity of
		local time, and the Markov property, for every nonnegative Borel function
		\(\varphi\) on \(\{(r,s):0<r<s<T\}\),
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			&\operatorname{E}_0\left[
			\int_0^T\int_0^s
			\varphi(r,s)\,d\ell_r^0\,d\ell_s^0
			\right]
			\\
			&\qquad=
			\operatorname{E}_0\left[
			\int_0^T
			\left(
			\int_r^T \varphi(r,s)\,d\ell_s^0
			\right)
			d\ell_r^0
			\right]
			\\
			&\qquad=
			\int_0^T
			p_r(0,0)
			\left(
			\int_0^{T-r}
			\varphi(r,r+u)\,
			p_u(0,0)\,du
			\right)dr
			\\
			&\qquad=
			\int_0^T\int_0^s
			\varphi(r,s)\,
			p_r(0,0)p_{s-r}(0,0)\,dr\,ds.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		
		Since \(\ell^0\) is continuous, its Stieltjes measure \(d\ell^0\) is
		atomless, and therefore \(d\ell^0\otimes d\ell^0\) gives no mass to the
		diagonal. Taking
		\[
		\varphi(r,s)=e^{-2a(s-r)/\varepsilon}
		\]
		and using symmetry, we obtain
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}\left|\int_0^T H_{s/\varepsilon}\,d\ell_s^0\right|^2
			&=
			2\int_{0<r<s<T}
			e^{-2a(s-r)/\varepsilon}
			p_r(0,0)p_{s-r}(0,0)\,dr\,ds
			\\
			&=
			2\int_0^T e^{-2au/\varepsilon}p_u(0,0)
			\int_0^{T-u}p_s(0,0)\,ds\,du
			\\
			&=
			\frac2\pi\int_0^T e^{-2au/\varepsilon}
			\sqrt{\frac{T-u}{u}}\,du
			\sim
			\sqrt{\frac{2T}{\pi a}}\,\varepsilon^{1/2}.
			\label{eq:interior-localtime-variance}
		\end{align}
		For the asymptotic, substitute $u=\varepsilon v$ and apply dominated
		convergence with the integrable bound
		\(\sqrt T\,e^{-2av}v^{-1/2}\). 
		
		By contrast, using the covariance formula~\eqref{eq:covariance_formula} with \(\lambda=2a/\varepsilon\),
		we get 
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}\left|\int_0^T H_{s/\varepsilon}\,ds\right|^2
			&=
			\int_0^T\int_0^T e^{-\lambda|s-r|}\,dr\,ds \\
			&=
			2\int_0^T \frac{1-e^{-\lambda s}}{\lambda}\,ds \\
			&=
			2\left(
			\frac{T}{\lambda}
			-
			\frac{1-e^{-\lambda T}}{\lambda^2}
			\right)
			\sim \frac{T}{a}\varepsilon.
			\label{eq:interior-occupationtime-variance}
		\end{align}
		The asymptotics~\eqref{eq:interior-localtime-variance} and
		\eqref{eq:interior-occupationtime-variance} show that ordinary occupation
		and local-time occupation fluctuate on different scales. In particular,
		within this class the exponent \(1/2\) in the terminal-time second-moment
		estimate for local-time occupation cannot be improved.

body_md:
\label{rem:abstract-boundary-local-time}
		Unlike the one-dimensional interior-local-time benchmark of
		Example~\ref{ex:abstract-benchmarks}, we consider here the boundary
		local time of reflected Brownian motion in a \(C^2\) domain \(D\).
		Appendix~\ref{app:averaging} shows that \(\vartheta=1/2\) in this case.
		Consequently, the random-time squared \(L^2\) error is
		\(O(\varepsilon^{1/2})\), while the maximal error is
		\(O(\varepsilon^{1/2}(1+|\log\varepsilon|)^2)\), and hence
		\(O(\varepsilon^\zeta)\) for every \(0<\zeta<1/2\).
		
		By Lemma~\ref{lem:AF-conditioning}, the first-moment estimate for the
		boundary local time also yields, for every finite \(q\ge1\),
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}\operatorname{E}_x[L_t^q]
		\le C_{T,q}t^{q/2},
		\qquad 0\le t\le T,
		\]
		and
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}_x[(L_v-L_u)^q]
		\le C_{T,q}(v-u)^{q/2},
		\qquad 0\le u<v\le T.
		\]
		Thus no additional moment assumption on the boundary local time is
		required beyond the short-time first-moment estimate.

body_md:
\label{def:SR_EK}
	We use the following terminology and associated smooth boundary classes.
	\begin{enuroman}
		\item The instantaneously reflected Brownian motion corresponds to
		\[
		\mathcal L^0 f=\frac12\Delta f,
		\qquad
		\partial_{\mathbf n}f=0
		\quad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		
		\item The homogeneous sticky reflected Brownian motion with parameter
		\(\rho\) corresponds to
		\[
		\mathcal L^{\mathrm{sticky}}f=\frac12\Delta f,
		\qquad
		\frac{\rho}{2}\Delta f+\partial_{\mathbf n}f=0
		\quad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		
		\item The homogeneous sticky reflected Brownian motion with elastic
		killing parameters \((\rho,\kappa)\) corresponds to
		\[
		\mathcal L^{\mathrm{el-sticky}}f=\frac12\Delta f,
		\qquad
		\frac{\rho}{2}\Delta f
		+\partial_{\mathbf n}f
		+\kappa f=0
		\quad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
	\end{enuroman}

body_md:
\label{prop:operational-time-process}
		The killed process
		\[
		\mathcal Y_t
		:=
		\begin{cases}
			(X_t, I_t),&t<\zeta,\\
			\dagger,&t\ge\zeta,
		\end{cases}
		\]
		is a c\`adl\`ag strong Markov process on
		\[
		E_\dagger
		:=
		(\overline D \times S)\cup\{\dagger\}.
		\]
		For every \(\Phi\in B_b(E)\), its family of sub-Markov transition operators is characterized by
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:construction-semigroup}
			(\mathcal S_t\Phi)(x,i)
			=
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\Phi(X_t,I_t)\mathbf 1_{\{t<\zeta\}}
			\right]
			=
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\Phi\!\left(W^+_{\gamma(t)},\alpha_{\gamma(t)}\right)
			e^{-K(t)}
			\right], 
		\end{equation}
		$t\ge0 $, $(i,x)\in E $.

title: Proof
body_md:
The independent processes \(W^+\) and \(\alpha\) are strong Markov, hence
		their product
		\[
		Z_t=(W_t^+,\alpha_t)
		\]
		is a c\`adl\`ag strong Markov process on
		\(E=\overline D\times S\).
		Its path regularity follows from the continuity of \(W^+\) and the
		c\`adl\`ag paths of \(\alpha\).
		
		\emph{Step 1: Applying the time-change.} The clock
		\[
		A(t)=t+\int_0^t\rho(\alpha_s)\,dL_s
		\]
		is a continuous additive functional of \(Z\), by the additivity of the
		boundary local time. Moreover, for \(0\le s\le t\),
		\[
		A(t)-A(s)
		=
		t-s+\int_s^t\rho(\alpha_u)\,dL_u
		\ge t-s.
		\]
		Hence \(A\) is strictly increasing and tends to infinity, and its inverse
		\(\gamma\) is finite, continuous, nondecreasing, and \(1\)-Lipschitz:
		\[
		A(\gamma(t))=t,
		\qquad
		|\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)|\le |t-s|.
		\]
		
		The inverse clock satisfies the usual composition rule
		\[
		\gamma(t+s)
		=
		\gamma(t)+\gamma(s)\circ\theta_{\gamma(t)},
		\]
		as well as the corresponding stopping-time version; see
		\cite[Chapter~V, Proposition~2.3]{BlumenthalGetor68}.
		
		By the standard time-change theorem for continuous additive functionals,
		the process
		\[
		\widehat Z_t:=Z_{\gamma(t)}
		=
		\bigl(W^+_{\gamma(t)},\alpha_{\gamma(t)}\bigr)
		=
		(X_t,I_t)
		\]
		is strong Markov with respect to the time-changed filtration
		\[
		\widehat{\mathcal F}_t=\mathcal F_{\gamma(t)};
		\]
		see \cite[Chapter~V, Proposition~2.3 and Exercise~2.11]{BlumenthalGetor68} or \cite[Theorem~10.10]{dynkin1965Markov_processes}.
		
		\emph{Step 2: Applying the killing functional.} Since \(\gamma\) is continuous and nondecreasing, \(X_t=W^+_{\gamma(t)}\)
		is continuous and \(I_t=\alpha_{\gamma(t)}\) is c\`adl\`ag. Hence
		\(\widehat Z=(X,I)\) is c\`adl\`ag.
		
		Define the operational-time killing functional
		\[
		B(t):=\int_0^t\kappa(\alpha_s)\,dL_s.
		\]
		Then \(B\) is a continuous additive functional of \(Z\), and
		\[
		K(t)=B(\gamma(t)).
		\]
		By the inverse-clock composition rule,
		\[
		K(t+s)=K(t)+K(s)\circ\widehat\theta_t,
		\]
		with the corresponding stopping-time version. Consequently,
		\[
		M_t:=e^{-K(t)}
		\]
		is a continuous strong multiplicative functional of \(\widehat Z\); see
		\cite[Chapter~III, Definition~3.11]{BlumenthalGetor68}.
		
		The standard multiplicative-functional construction therefore yields the
		killed subprocess
		\[
		\mathcal Y_t=
		\begin{cases}
			(X_t,I_t),&t<\zeta,\\
			\dagger,&t\ge\zeta,
		\end{cases}
		\]
		which is a c\`adl\`ag strong Markov process; see
		\cite[Chapter~III, Theorem~3.3 and Proposition~3.12]{BlumenthalGetor68}.
		
		
		\emph{Step 3: Identification of transition law.} 
		Since \(K(t)\) is measurable with respect to the path of \(Z\), independence
		of \(\mathcal E\sim\operatorname{Exp}(1)\) gives
		\[
		\operatorname{P}(t<\zeta\mid \sigma(Z_s:s\ge0))
		=
		\operatorname{P}(\mathcal E\ge K(t)\mid \sigma(Z_s:s\ge0))
		=
		e^{-K(t)}.
		\]
		Hence, for every bounded Borel function \(\Phi\),
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\Phi(X_t,I_t)\mathbf 1_{\{t<\zeta\}}
			\right]
			&=
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\Phi(X_t,I_t)e^{-K(t)}
			\right]
			\\
			&=
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\Phi\!\left(
			W^+_{\gamma(t)},\alpha_{\gamma(t)}
			\right)
			e^{-K(t)}
			\right].
		\end{align}
		This is \eqref{eq:construction-semigroup}.

title: Remark
body_md:
The construction also admits a segment-by-segment interpretation.
		While the regime is \(i\), the reflected motion evolves with clock
		\(s+\rho_iL_s\), until either the Markov chain leaves state \(i\) or
		elastic killing occurs through the local-time hazard
		\(\kappa_i\,dL_s\). At a switching event the spatial position is
		unchanged and the evolution continues in the new regime. 
		This is consistent with the classical piecing-out viewpoint of
		Ikeda--Nagasawa--Watanabe
		\cite{ikeda1996_construction_piecingout}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Again, \(C\) may change from line to line but is independent of
	\(\varepsilon\) and uniform in \(x\in\overline D\).
	
	\medskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: the killing functional.}
	Fix \(\beta\in(0,1/8)\) and choose \(\theta\in(0,1/2)\) so that
	\[
	\beta<\frac{\theta}{4}.
	\]
	For deterministic \(t\in[0,T]\), we split
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)
		&=
		\int_0^{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}
		\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})\,dL_s
		-
		\overline\kappa L_{\gamma_0(t)}
		\\
		&=
		\int_0^{\gamma_0(t)}
		\bigl(\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline\kappa\bigr)\,dL_s
		+
		\int_{\gamma_0(t)}^{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}
		\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})\,dL_s,
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	where the second integral is understood in the oriented sense.
	Hence
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:fixed-time-killing-bound}
		|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|
		\le
		\left|
		\int_0^{\gamma_0(t)}
		\bigl(\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline\kappa\bigr)\,dL_s
		\right|
		+
		\|\kappa\|_\infty
		|L_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}-L_{\gamma_0(t)}|.
	\end{equation}
	
	The first term in \eqref{eq:fixed-time-killing-bound} is an averaged
	local-time integral. Since \(\gamma_0(t)\) depends only on the reflected
	path and is bounded by \(T\), the random-time averaging estimate
	\eqref{eq:local-time-averaging-assumption-nonmax}, which is uniform in the
	starting point, together with Lyapunov's inequality gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:fixed-time-kappa-average-L1}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		\left|
		\int_0^{\gamma_0(t)}
		\bigl(\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline\kappa\bigr)\,dL_s
		\right|
		\right]
		\le
		C\varepsilon^{1/4}.
	\end{equation}
	
	For the second term in \eqref{eq:fixed-time-killing-bound}, the H\"older
	seminorm of \(L\) gives
	\[
	|L_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}-L_{\gamma_0(t)}|
	\le
	[L]_{\theta,T}
	|\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)|^\theta
	=
	[L]_{\theta,T}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta,
	\]
	where
	\[
	\Delta_\varepsilon(t)
	:=
	|\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)|.
	\]
	Choose \(q>1\) with \(\theta q\le2\), and let \(q'\) be conjugate to \(q\).
	H\"older's inequality gives
	\[
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	[L]_{\theta,T}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta
	\right]
	\le
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[[L]_{\theta,T}^{q'}\right]^{1/q'}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^{\theta q}
	\right]^{1/q}.
	\]
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:Holder},
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[[L]_{\theta,T}^{q'}\right]
	<\infty,
	\]
	while \eqref{eq:fixed-time-gamma-La-rate} controls the second factor:
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\sup_{0\le t\le T}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^{\theta q}
	\right]^{1/q}
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{\theta/4}.
	\]
	Therefore,
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:fixed-time-local-time-shift-rate}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		[L]_{\theta,T}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta
		\right]
		\le
		C\varepsilon^{\theta/4}.
	\end{equation}
	Combining \eqref{eq:fixed-time-killing-bound},
	\eqref{eq:fixed-time-kappa-average-L1}, and
	\eqref{eq:fixed-time-local-time-shift-rate} gives
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\sup_{0\le t\le T}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|
	\right]
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{1/4}+C\varepsilon^{\theta/4}.
	\]
	Since \(\beta<\theta/4<1/4\), this yields
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:fixed-time-killing-rate}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|
		\right]
		\le
		C\varepsilon^\beta.
	\end{equation}
	
	\medskip
	\noindent\emph{Step 2: the Feynman--Kac weights.}
	Define
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:Y-epsilon-Y-zero}
		Y_\varepsilon(t)
		:=
		f\left(W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}\right)e^{-K_\varepsilon(t)},
		\qquad
		Y_0(t)
		:=
		f\left(W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}\right)e^{-K_0(t)}.
	\end{equation}
	Inserting the mixed term
	\(f(W^+_{\gamma_0(t)})e^{-K_\varepsilon(t)}\) and splitting gives
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)
		&=
		\left[
		f\left(W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}\right)
		-
		f\left(W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}\right)
		\right]e^{-K_\varepsilon(t)}
		\\
		&\quad
		+
		f\left(W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}\right)
		\left[
		e^{-K_\varepsilon(t)}-e^{-K_0(t)}
		\right].
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	Using \(e^{-K_\varepsilon(t)}\le1\), the Lipschitz continuity of \(f\),
	and the fact that \(r\mapsto e^{-r}\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz on
	\([0,\infty)\), we obtain
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:Y-difference-bound}
		|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
		\le
		\mathrm{Lip}(f)
		\left|
		W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}
		-
		W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}
		\right|
		+
		\|f\|_\infty
		|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|.
	\end{equation}
	Taking expectations and using
	Proposition~\ref{thm:sticky}\ref{item:sticky_marginal} with \(p=1\),
	together with \eqref{eq:fixed-time-killing-rate}, gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:fixed-time-Y-rate}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
		\right]
		\le
		C\varepsilon^\beta.
	\end{equation}
	
	\medskip
	\noindent\emph{Step 3: quenched evolution.}
	For fixed \(\alpha\), \eqref{eq:quenched-semigroup} and
	\eqref{eq:limit-semigroup} give
	\[
	u^\varepsilon_\alpha(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
	=
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[
	Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)
	\right].
	\]
	Hence, for every \(t\in[0,T]\),
	\[
	|u^\varepsilon_\alpha(t,x)-u^0(t,x)|
	\le
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[
	|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
	\right].
	\]
	Average now over \(\alpha\), take the supremum over deterministic \(t\),
	and then over \(x\in\overline D\):
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		&\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}^\alpha
		\left[
		|u^\varepsilon_\alpha(t,x)-u^0(t,x)|
		\right]
		\\
		&\qquad\le
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}^\alpha
		\operatorname{E}_x^W
		\left[
		|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
		\right]
		\\
		&\qquad=
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}
		\left[
		|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
		\right],
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	which combined with \eqref{eq:fixed-time-Y-rate} gives
	\eqref{eq:semigroup-rate-nonmax}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Again, \(C\) may change from line to line but is independent of
	\(\varepsilon\) and uniform in \(x\in\overline D\). Fix \(0<\beta<1/8\) and choose
	\(0<\zeta<1/2\) and \(\theta<1/2\) so that
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:choose-theta-zeta-SE}
		\beta<\frac{\theta\zeta}{2}.
	\end{equation}
	
	For fixed \(\alpha\),
	\[
	\sup_{t\in[0,T]}
	|u^\varepsilon_\alpha(t,x)-u^0(t,x)|
	\le
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[
	\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
	\right].
	\]
	Averaging over \(\alpha\) and taking the supremum over
	\(x\in\overline D\) gives
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:uniform-quenched-joint-bound}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}^\alpha\left[
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|u^\varepsilon_\alpha(t,x)-u^0(t,x)|
		\right]
		\le
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
		\right].
	\end{equation}
	By~\eqref{eq:Y-difference-bound},
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:quenched_Wentzell_split}
		\begin{aligned}
			\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|Y_\varepsilon(t)-Y_0(t)|
			&\le
			\mathrm{Lip}(f)
			\sup_{t\in[0,T]}
			|W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}-W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}|\\
			&\quad+
			\|f\|_\infty
			\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|.
		\end{aligned}
	\end{equation}
	Proposition~\ref{thm:sticky}\ref{item:sticky_uniform} yields
	\begin{equation}
		\label{eq:uniform-space-error-L1}
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}
		|W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}-W^+_{\gamma_0(t)}|
		\right]
		\le C\varepsilon^\beta.
	\end{equation}
	
	For the killing term, the same decomposition as before gives
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|
		&\le
		\sup_{r\in[0,T]}
		\left|
		\int_0^r
		\bigl(\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline\kappa\bigr)\,dL_s
		\right|\\
		&\quad+
		\|\kappa\|_\infty [L]_{\theta,T}
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	By~\eqref{eq:local-time-averaging-assumption-max} and Lyapunov's inequality,
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	\sup_{r\in[0,T]}
	\left|
	\int_0^r
	\bigl(\kappa(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\overline\kappa\bigr)\,dL_s
	\right|
	\right]
	\le C\varepsilon^{\zeta/2}.
	\]
	Choose \(r>1\) such that \(\theta r\le2\), and let \(r'\) be its conjugate
	exponent. By H\"older's inequality,
	\eqref{eq:Kolmogorov_regularity}, and
	\eqref{eq:uniform-gamma-La-rate},
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		&\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		[L]_{\theta,T}
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta
		\right]\\
		&\qquad\le
		\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[[L]_{\theta,T}^{r'}\right]^{1/r'}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
		\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^{\theta r}
		\right]^{1/r}.
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	By Proposition~\ref{prop:Holder},
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_x^W\left[[L]_{\theta,T}^{r'}\right]
	<\infty,
	\]
	while \eqref{eq:uniform-gamma-La-rate} gives
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^{\theta r}
	\right]^{1/r}
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{\theta\zeta/2}.
	\]
	Therefore,
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	[L]_{\theta,T}
	\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\Delta_\varepsilon(t)^\theta
	\right]
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{\theta\zeta/2}.
	\]
	Consequently, by \eqref{eq:choose-theta-zeta-SE},
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}\left[
	\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|K_\varepsilon(t)-K_0(t)|
	\right]
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{\zeta/2}+C\varepsilon^{\theta\zeta/2}
	\le C\varepsilon^\beta.
	\]
	Combining the above with
	\eqref{eq:uniform-quenched-joint-bound},
	\eqref{eq:quenched_Wentzell_split}, and
	\eqref{eq:uniform-space-error-L1}
	gives \eqref{eq:semigroup-rate}.

label: prop:boundary-LT-sharpness
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:boundary-LT-sharpness}
		Let \(D=(0,1)\), and let \(W^+\) be reflected Brownian motion on
		\(\overline D=[0,1]\), with generator
		\(\frac12\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\), started from \(0\).
		Write \(L^{(0)}\) and \(L^{(1)}\) for the regulators at \(0\) and \(1\),
		respectively, so that
		\[
		L=L^{(0)}+L^{(1)}
		\]
		is the total boundary local time.
		
		Let \(S=\{1,2\}\), and let \(\alpha\) be the independent Markov chain
		with generator
		\[
		Q
		=
		\begin{pmatrix}
			-a&a\\
			a&-a
		\end{pmatrix},
		\qquad a>0.
		\]
		Its invariant distribution is
		\[
		\pi=\left(\frac12,\frac12\right).
		\]
		Assume \(\alpha_0\sim\pi\), and set
		\[
		h(1)=-1,
		\qquad
		h(2)=1.
		\]
		Then \(\pi(h)=0\) and
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_\pi^\alpha
		\left[
		h(\alpha_t)h(\alpha_s)
		\right]
		=
		e^{-2a|t-s|}.
		\]
		
		For
		\[
		J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
		:=
		\int_0^T
		h(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})\,dL_s^{(0)}
		= \int_0^T
		\left(h(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon}) - \pi(h) \right)\,dL_s^{(0)},
		\]
		we have, for every \(T>0\),
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:boundary-LT-sharpness}
			\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
			\left|
			J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
			\right|^2
			\sim
			\frac{\operatorname{E}_0[L_T^{(0)}]}{\sqrt a}\,
			\varepsilon^{1/2},
			\qquad
			\varepsilon\downarrow0.
		\end{equation}
		In particular, the exponent \(1/2\) in the squared \(L^2\)
		random-time averaging estimate cannot be improved in general.
		
		For the total boundary local time,
		\[
		J_\varepsilon(T)
		:=
		\int_0^T
		h(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})\,dL_s,
		\]
		there exist constants \(0<c_T\le C_T<\infty\) such that
		\[
		c_T\varepsilon^{1/2}
		\le
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
		\left|
		J_\varepsilon(T)
		\right|^2
		\le
		C_T\varepsilon^{1/2}
		\]
		for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\).
		
		In particular, the exponent \(1/2\) in the boundary-local-time averaging estimate \eqref{eq:local-time-averaging-assumption-nonmax} cannot be improved in general.

title: Proof
body_md:
This is a specialization of
		Theorem~\ref{thm:abstract-averaging} with
		\[
		A=L^{(0)}.
		\]
		Since \(\pi(h)=0\),
		\[
		J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
		=
		\int_0^T
		\bigl(
		h(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})-\pi(h)
		\bigr)\,dL_s^{(0)}.
		\]
		The theorem gives the upper bound of order
		\(\varepsilon^{1/2}\). We show that this order is attained.
		
		Let \(p^{W^+}(t,x,y)\) be the reflected heat kernel on \([0,1]\).
		With our normalization, \(L^{(0)}\) is the PCAF in Revuz
		correspondence with the "surface" measure \(\frac12\delta_0\). Conditioning on the reflected
		path and using stationarity of \(\alpha\),
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
		\left|
		J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
		\right|^2
		=
		\operatorname{E}_0
		\int_0^T\int_0^T
		e^{-2a|s-r|/\varepsilon}\,
		dL_r^{(0)}\,dL_s^{(0)}.
		\]
		The diagonal carries no
		\(dL^{(0)}\otimes dL^{(0)}\)-mass. By symmetry, the Markov property,
		and the Revuz formula,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:boundary-LT-double-kernel}
			\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
			\left|
			J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
			\right|^2
			=
			\frac12
			\int_0^T
			p^{W^+}(r,0,0)
			\int_0^{T-r}
			e^{-2au/\varepsilon}
			p^{W^+}(u,0,0)\,du\,dr .
		\end{equation}
		
		The image representation of the reflected heat kernel gives
		\[
		p^{W^+}(u,0,0)
		=
		\frac{2}{\sqrt{2\pi u}}
		\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z}
		\exp\left(-\frac{2k^2}{u}\right).
		\]
		Since the \(k=0\) term dominates as \(u\downarrow0\),
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:Neumann-small-time-boundary}
			p^{W^+}(u,0,0)
			\sim
			\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi u}},
			\qquad u\downarrow0.
		\end{equation}
		and, for every fixed \(T>0\),
		\[
		p^{W^+}(u,0,0)
		\le
		C_Tu^{-1/2},
		\qquad
		0<u\le T.
		\]
		
		For \(R>0\), put
		\[
		I_\varepsilon(R)
		:=
		\int_0^R
		e^{-2au/\varepsilon}
		p^{W^+}(u,0,0)\,du,
		\]
		so that
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:boundary-LT-double-kernel_2}
			\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
			\left|
			J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
			\right|^2
			= 
			\frac12
			\int_0^T
			p^{W^+}(r,0,0)
			I_\varepsilon(T-r) \,dr .
		\end{equation}
		With \(u=\varepsilon v\),
		\[
		\frac{I_\varepsilon(R)}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
		=
		\sqrt\varepsilon
		\int_0^{R/\varepsilon}
		e^{-2av}
		p^{W^+}(\varepsilon v,0,0)\,dv.
		\]
		By \eqref{eq:Neumann-small-time-boundary} and dominated convergence,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:sharpness_proof_dom1}
			\frac{I_\varepsilon(R)}{\sqrt\varepsilon}
			\longrightarrow
			\sqrt{\frac2\pi}
			\int_0^\infty
			e^{-2av}v^{-1/2}\,dv
			=
			\frac1{\sqrt a}.
		\end{equation}
		Moreover, the heat-kernel bound gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:sharpness_proof_dom2}
			\sup_{0<R\le T}
			\frac{I_\varepsilon(R)}{\sqrt{\varepsilon}}
			\le C_{T,a},
			\qquad 0<\varepsilon\le1.
		\end{equation}
		
		By~\eqref{eq:sharpness_proof_dom1} and \eqref{eq:sharpness_proof_dom2}, we can apply the dominated convergence to~\eqref{eq:boundary-LT-double-kernel_2}, which yields
		\[
		\varepsilon^{-1/2}
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}
		\left|
		J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)
		\right|^2
		\longrightarrow
		\frac1{2\sqrt a}
		\int_0^T
		p^{W^+}(r,0,0)\,dr.
		\]
		By the Revuz formula,
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_0[L_T^{(0)}]
		=
		\frac12
		\int_0^T
		p^{W^+}(r,0,0)\,dr,
		\]
		which proves \eqref{eq:boundary-LT-sharpness}.
		
		For \(L=L^{(0)}+L^{(1)}\), conditioning on \(W^+\) gives
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}|J_\varepsilon(T)|^2
		=
		\operatorname{E}_0
		\int_0^T\int_0^T
		e^{-2a|s-r|/\varepsilon}\,dL_r\,dL_s.
		\]
		Since the covariance kernel is nonnegative and
		\[
		dL=dL^{(0)}+dL^{(1)},
		\]
		all four contributions in the expansion are nonnegative. Hence
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}|J_\varepsilon(T)|^2
		\ge
		\operatorname{E}_{0,\pi}|J_\varepsilon^{(0)}(T)|^2
		\ge c_T\varepsilon^{1/2}
		\]
		for all sufficiently small \(\varepsilon\), by
		\eqref{eq:boundary-LT-sharpness}.
		The upper bound follows from
		Theorem~\ref{thm:abstract-averaging} with \(A=L\) and
		\(\vartheta=1/2\).

\label{rem:boundary-LT-max-sharpness}

		\sup_{0\le t\le T}

label: thm:improved-smooth-observable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:improved-smooth-observable}
		Assume that, for some \(c\ge0\),
		\[
		\kappa_i=c\rho_i,
		\qquad i\in S,
		\]
		and let \(f\in C^2(\overline D)\) satisfy
		\[
		\partial_{\mathbf n}f=0
		\qquad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		Then, for every \(T>0\),
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:smooth-observable-fixed-rate}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D} \sup_{0\le t\le T}
			\operatorname{E}^\alpha
			\left|
			u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
			\right|
			\le
			C\varepsilon^{1/4},
		\end{equation}
		and
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:smooth-observable-max-rate}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D} \operatorname{E}^\alpha
			\left[
			\sup_{0\le t\le T}
			\left|
			u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
			\right|
			\right]
			\le
			C\varepsilon^{1/4}
			\bigl(1+|\log\varepsilon|\bigr).
		\end{equation}
		In particular, the second estimate is
		\(O(\varepsilon^\beta)\) for every \(\beta<1/4\).
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since \(\kappa_i=c\rho_i\) for every \(i\), and since \(A_\varepsilon(\gamma_\varepsilon(t))=t\), 
	\[
	K_\varepsilon(t)
	=
	c\int_0^{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}
	\rho(\alpha_{s/\varepsilon})\,dL_s
	=
	c\bigl(t-\gamma_\varepsilon(t)\bigr).
	\]
	Since also \(\overline\kappa=c\overline\rho\),
	\[
	K_0(t)
	=
	c\bigl(t-\gamma_0(t)\bigr).
	\]
	Therefore
	\[
	u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)
	=
	e^{-ct}
	\operatorname{E}_x^W
	\left[
	e^{c\gamma_\varepsilon(t)}
	f(W^+_{\gamma_\varepsilon(t)})
	\right],
	\]
	and similarly
	\[
	u^0(t,x)
	=
	e^{-ct}
	\operatorname{E}_x^W
	\left[
	e^{c\gamma_0(t)}
	f(W^+_{\gamma_0(t)})
	\right].
	\]
	
	Fix \(\alpha\) and \(t\in[0,T]\). The two inverse clocks are bounded
	stopping times for the reflected Brownian filtration. Define
	\[
	F(s,x):=e^{cs}f(x).
	\]
	Applying It\^o's formula to the process
	\[
	F(s,W_s^+)=e^{cs}f(W_s^+),
	\]
	and using \(f\in C^2(\overline D)\) together with
	\(\partial_{\mathbf n}f=0\), the boundary local-time term vanishes.
	Thus, for every such stopping time \(\tau\),
	\[
	\operatorname{E}_x^W
	\left[
	e^{c\tau}f(W_\tau^+)
	\right]
	=
	f(x)
	+
	\operatorname{E}_x^W
	\int_0^\tau
	e^{cs}
	\left(
	cf+\frac12\Delta f
	\right)(W_s^+)\,ds.
	\]
	
	Applying this identity with
	\(\tau=\gamma_\varepsilon(t)\) and \(\tau=\gamma_0(t)\),
	subtracting the resulting expressions, and using the representations above,
	we obtain
	\[
	|u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)|
	\le
	C_f\operatorname{E}_x^W
	|\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)|.
	\]
	
	Averaging the preceding estimate over the environment and taking the
	supremum over \(x\in\overline D\) gives
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		&\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}^\alpha
		\left|
		u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
		\right|
		\\
		&\qquad\le
		C_f
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}
		\left|
		\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)
		\right|
		\\
		&\qquad\le
		C_f
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		\left(
		\operatorname{E}_{x,\pi}
		\left|
		\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)
		\right|^2
		\right)^{1/2}
		\\
		&\qquad\le
		C\varepsilon^{1/4},
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	where the second inequality is Lyapunov's inequality and the last one follows
	from~\eqref{eq:fixed-time-gamma-L2-rate}.
	
	For the uniform estimate, the same argument gives
	\[
	\sup_{0\le t\le T}
	\left|
	u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
	\right|
	\le
	C_f
	\operatorname{E}_x^W
	\left[
	\sup_{0\le t\le T}
	|\gamma_\varepsilon(t)-\gamma_0(t)|
	\right].
	\]
	The maximal estimate of
	Theorem~\ref{thm:abstract-averaging}, with
	\(\vartheta=1/2\), followed by Lyapunov's inequality, yields
	\[
	\sup_{x\in\overline D}
	\operatorname{E}^\alpha
	\left[
	\sup_{0\le t\le T}
	\left|
	u_\alpha^\varepsilon(t,x)-u^0(t,x)
	\right|
	\right]
	\le
	C\varepsilon^{1/4}
	\bigl(1+|\log\varepsilon|\bigr).
	\]
	This completes the proof.

body_md:
Proposition~\ref{prop:boundary-LT-sharpness} shows that the
		\(\varepsilon^{1/2}\) second-moment boundary-local-time averaging rate is sharp, but
		this does not imply that the resulting observable rates are optimal.
		Under the proportionality condition of
		Theorem~\ref{thm:improved-smooth-observable}, one obtains the better

label: lem:reflected-start-continuity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:reflected-start-continuity}
		On a bounded $C^2$ domain, couple normally reflected Brownian motions $W^x,W^y$ using the same Brownian driver, with regulators $L^x,L^y$ normalized as in Section~\ref{ssec:notation}: 
		\begin{equation}
			W_t^{x}
			=
			x+B_t-\int_0^t \mathbf n(W_s^x)\,dL_s^x,
			\qquad
			W_t^{y}
			=
			y+B_t-\int_0^t \mathbf n(W_s^y)\,dL_s^y,
			\qquad t\ge0.
		\end{equation}
		For every $T>0$, as $y\to x$,
		\[
		\sup_{s\le T}|W_s^y-W_s^x|+\sup_{s\le T}|L_s^y-L_s^x|
		\longrightarrow0\quad\text{in probability}.
		\]
head: environment
name: Continuity in initial position

title: Proof
body_md:
Set $Z_t := W^{x}_t - W^{y}_t $. 
		Under common-noise coupling,
		\[
		d Z_t
		=
		-\mathbf n(W_t^x)\,dL_t^x
		+\mathbf n(W_t^y)\,dL_t^y.
		\]
		Since \(D\) is bounded with \(C^2\) boundary, it satisfies a uniform
		exterior sphere condition; see, e.g.,
		\cite[Chapter~2, Problem~2.11]{gilbarg2001_elliptic_PDEs}.
		Hence, by \cite[Condition~(A) and Remark~1.1]{saisho1987stochastic},
		there exists \(c_D>0\) such that
		\[
		(z-w)\cdot\mathbf n(z)
		\ge -c_D|z-w|^2,
		\qquad z\in\partial D,\quad w\in\overline D.
		\]
		
		Under the common-noise coupling,
		\[
		dZ_t
		=
		-\mathbf n(W_t^x)\,dL_t^x
		+\mathbf n(W_t^y)\,dL_t^y.
		\]
		Since \(Z\) has finite variation,
		\[
		d|Z_t|^2
		=
		-2 Z_t\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^x)\,dL_t^x
		+2 Z_t\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^y)\,dL_t^y.
		\]
		Now \(dL_t^x\) is carried by \(\{W_t^x\in\partial D\}\), so on its support,
		\[
		Z_t\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^x)
		=
		(W_t^x-W_t^y)\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^x)
		\ge -c_D|Z_t|^2.
		\]
		Likewise, since \(dL_t^y\) is carried by \(\{W_t^y\in\partial D\}\),
		\[
		(W_t^y-W_t^x)\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^y)
		\ge -c_D|Z_t|^2,
		\]
		or equivalently
		\[
		Z_t\cdot \mathbf n(W_t^y)
		\le c_D|Z_t|^2.
		\]
		Therefore
		\[
		d|Z_t|^2
		\le
		2c_D|Z_t|^2\,(dL_t^x+dL_t^y).
		\]
		And hence, Gr\"onwall's inequality (see, e.g., \cite[Lemma~2.2]{saisho1987stochastic}) gives
		\[
		\sup_{s\le T}|W_s^x-W_s^y|^2
		\le
		|x-y|^2
		\exp\!\left\{2c_D(L_T^x+L_T^y)\right\}.
		\]
		
		By Lemma~\ref{lem:short-time-growth-local-time},
		\[
		C_T:=\sup_{z\in\overline D}\operatorname{E}_z L_T<\infty.
		\]
		Hence, for every \(R>0\), Markov's inequality gives
		\[
		\sup_{x,y\in\overline D}
		\Pr\!\left(L_T^x+L_T^y>R\right)
		\le \frac{2C_T}{R}.
		\]
		Thus \(\{L_T^x+L_T^y:x,y\in\overline D\}\) is tight; see
		\cite[Section~5]{billingsley1968Convergence_of}.
		Combining this with the preceding estimate yields
		\[
		\sup_{s\le T}|W_s^x-W_s^y|\longrightarrow0
		\qquad\text{in probability as }y\to x.
		\]
		
		
		For the local time convergence, we use the smooth distance function
		\(r\) described in Appendix~\ref{app:Holder_continuity}: it belongs to
		\(C^2(\overline D)\), agrees with the inward distance in a collar of
		\(\partial D\), and satisfies
		\[
		\nabla r\cdot\mathbf n=-1
		\qquad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		It\^o's formula gives
		\[
		L_t^x
		=
		r(W_t^x)-r(x)
		-\int_0^t \nabla r(W_s^x)\cdot dB_s
		-\frac12\int_0^t \Delta r(W_s^x)\,ds.
		\]
		Subtracting the corresponding identity for \(y\), the uniform continuity
		of \(r\) and \(\Delta r\), together with the preceding path convergence,
		shows that the non-martingale terms converge uniformly in probability.
		Moreover, by the BDG inequality,
		\[
		\operatorname{E}\!\left[
		\sup_{t\le T}
		\left|
		\int_0^t
		\bigl(\nabla r(W_s^x)-\nabla r(W_s^y)\bigr)\cdot dB_s
		\right|^2
		\right]
		\le
		C\,\operatorname{E}\int_0^T
		\left|\nabla r(W_s^x)-\nabla r(W_s^y)\right|^2 ds.
		\]
		The right-hand side tends to zero because \(\nabla r\) is bounded and
		uniformly continuous and
		\(\sup_{s\le T}|W_s^x-W_s^y|\to0\) in probability. Hence
		\[
		\sup_{t\le T}|L_t^x-L_t^y|
		\longrightarrow0
		\qquad\text{in probability}.
		\]
		This completes the proof.

label: thm:quenched_sticky_elastic
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:quenched_sticky_elastic}
		The family \((S_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}\) defined by
		\eqref{eq:quenched-spatial-operator} has the following properties.
		
		\begin{enumerate}
			\item (Preservation of continuity, contractivity, and continuity at the origin.) For every \(t\ge0\),
			\[
			S^{\alpha}_t f\in C(\overline D), \quad 
			\|S_t^\alpha f\|_\infty
			\le
			\|f\|_\infty,
			\quad f\in C(\overline D).
			\]
			Moreover,
			\[
			\|S_t^\alpha f-f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0,
			\qquad t\downarrow0.
			\]
			
			\item (Dynkin formula.) For every \(f\in C^2(\overline D)\),
			\begin{equation}
				\label{eq:quenched-backward-dynkin}
				\begin{aligned}
					(S_t^\alpha f)(x)-f(x)
					&=
					\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
					\frac12
					\int_0^{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
					H^\alpha_s
					\Delta f(W_s^+)\,ds
					\right]
					\\
					&\quad
					-
					\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
					\int_0^{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
					H^\alpha_s
					\left(
					\partial_{\mathbf n}f
					+\kappa(\alpha_s)f
					\right)(W_s^+)\,dL_s
					\right].
				\end{aligned}
			\end{equation}
			
			\item (Quenched backward equation.) If \(f\in\mathcal D_\alpha\), then
			\begin{equation}
				\label{eq:quenched-backward-mild}
				S_t^\alpha f
				=
				f+\frac12\int_0^t S_s^\alpha(\Delta f)\,ds,
				\qquad t\ge0.
			\end{equation}
			In particular, the map \(t\mapsto S_t^\alpha f\) is continuously
			differentiable and satisfies
			\begin{equation}
				\label{eq:quenched-backward-derivative}
				\frac{d}{dt}S_t^\alpha f
				=
				\frac12S_t^\alpha(\Delta f),
				\qquad t\ge0.
			\end{equation}
		\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: eq:quenched-strong-continuity-bound
title: Proof
body_md:
\medskip\noindent\emph{1. Contractivity and continuity at the origin.}
		Since \(K^\alpha(t)\ge0\), for every \(f\in C(\overline D)\),
		\[
		|(S_t^\alpha f)(x)|
		\le
		\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
		\left|f\!\left(W^+_{\gamma^\alpha(t)}\right)\right|
		e^{-K^\alpha(t)}
		\right]
		\le
		\|f\|_\infty.
		\]
		For continuity at $t=0$, since
		\[
		0\le\gamma^\alpha(t)\le t,
		\]
		we have
		\begin{align}
			|(S_t^\alpha f)(x)-f(x)|
			&\le
			\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
			\left|
			f\!\left(W^+_{\gamma^\alpha(t)}\right)-f(x)
			\right|
			\right]
			\nonumber\\
			&\quad
			+
			\|f\|_\infty
			\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[1-e^{-K^\alpha(t)}\right].
			\label{eq:quenched-strong-continuity-bound}
		\end{align}
		The first term tends to zero uniformly in \(x\), by the uniform continuity
		of \(f\) and Proposition~\ref{prop:Holder}, which yields
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
		\sup_{0\le s\le t}|W_s^+-x|^q
		\right]
		\le C t^{q\theta}.
		\]
		
		For the second, \(1-e^{-z}\le z\) gives
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[1-e^{-K^\alpha(t)}\right]
		\le
		\|\kappa\|_\infty\operatorname{E}_x[L_t].
		\]
		Again by Proposition~\ref{prop:Holder},
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}\operatorname{E}_x[L_t]
		\le C t^\theta,
		\]
		so the right-hand side tends to zero uniformly in \(x\). Thus
		\[
		\|S_t^\alpha f-f\|_\infty\longrightarrow0
		\qquad\text{as }t\downarrow0.
		\]
		
		It remains to show that \(S_t^\alpha\) preserves continuity. Let \(x_n\to x\)
		and use the common-reference coupling from Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected-start-continuity}.
		Then, on every bounded operational-time interval,
		\[
		\sup_{s\le T}|W_s^{x_n}-W_s^x|
		+
		\sup_{s\le T}|L_s^{x_n}-L_s^x|
		\longrightarrow0
		\qquad\text{in probability}.
		\]
		Since the fixed path \(\alpha\) has only finitely many jumps on \([0,T]\),
		the weighted local-time integrals are finite sums of increments of \(L\);
		hence the corresponding clocks and killing functionals converge uniformly
		in probability. As the clocks are continuous and strictly increasing, their
		inverses converge uniformly on compact time intervals as well. Hence, for each
		fixed \(t\),
		\[
		e^{-K^{\alpha,x_n}(t)}
		f\!\left(W_{\gamma^{\alpha,x_n}(t)}^{x_n}\right)
		\longrightarrow
		e^{-K^{\alpha,x}(t)}
		f\!\left(W_{\gamma^{\alpha,x}(t)}^{x}\right)
		\]
		in probability. 
		Since these random variables are uniformly bounded by
		\(\|f\|_\infty\), the convergence also holds in \(L^1\), see, e.g., \cite[Theorem~4.6.3]{durrett2019probability}.  
		Thus,
		\[
		(S_t^\alpha f)(x_n)\to(S_t^\alpha f)(x).
		\]
		
		The same coupling argument, together with Proposition~\ref{prop:Holder} and
		the continuity of the inverse clocks, shows that
		\[
		(t,x)\longmapsto (S_t^\alpha f)(x)
		\]
		is jointly continuous on bounded time intervals. Since
		\([0,T]\times\overline D\) is compact, it follows that
		\(t\mapsto S_t^\alpha f\) is continuous in \(C(\overline D)\).
		
		\medskip\noindent\emph{2. Dynkin formula.}
		For $f\in C^2(\overline D)$, It\^o's formula with the outward normal
		convention gives
		\[
		f(W_s^+)-f(x)
		=
		\int_0^s\nabla f(W_u^+)\cdot dB_u
		+
		\frac12\int_0^s\Delta f(W_u^+)\,du
		-
		\int_0^s\partial_{\mathbf n}f(W_u^+)\,dL_u.
		\]
		Applying the product rule to
		\[
		H^\alpha_s f(W_s^+)
		\]
		and stopping at the bounded stopping time \(\gamma^\alpha(t)\le t\), we obtain
		\begin{align}
			&H^\alpha_{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
			f\!\left(W^+_{\gamma^\alpha(t)}\right)-f(x)
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			\mathcal N_t
			+
			\frac12
			\int_0^{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
			H^\alpha_s\Delta f(W_s^+)\,ds
			\nonumber\\
			&\quad
			-
			\int_0^{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
			H^\alpha_s
			\left(
			\partial_{\mathbf n}f
			+\kappa(\alpha_s)f
			\right)(W_s^+)\,dL_s,
			\label{eq:quenched-product-formula}
		\end{align}
		where $\mathcal N_t$ is a zero-mean martingale term. Since
		\[
		H^\alpha_{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
		=
		e^{-K^\alpha(t)},
		\]
		taking expectations gives \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-dynkin}.
		
		\medskip
		\noindent\emph{3. Quenched backward equation.}
		Let \(f\in\mathcal D_\alpha\). 
		Since \(dL_s\) is supported on \(\{W_s^+\in\partial D\}\), the boundary
		condition defining \(\mathcal D_\alpha\) gives, \(dL_s\)-a.e.,
		\[
		-
		\left(
		\partial_{\mathbf n}f+\kappa(\alpha_s)f
		\right)(W_s^+)
		=
		\frac{\rho(\alpha_s)}2
		\Delta f(W_s^+).
		\]
		Substitution into \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-dynkin} and the definition of $ A^{\alpha}$ yields
		\begin{align}
			(S_t^\alpha f)(x)-f(x)
			&=
			\frac12
			\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
			\int_0^{\gamma^\alpha(t)}
			H^\alpha_s\Delta f(W_s^+)
			\,dA^\alpha(s)
			\right].
			\label{eq:quenched-clock-integral}
		\end{align}
		Since \(A^\alpha\) is continuous and strictly increasing and
		\[
		A^\alpha(\gamma^\alpha(t))=t,
		\]
		the change of variables \(u=A^\alpha(s)\) gives
		\begin{align}
			(S_t^\alpha f)(x)-f(x)
			&=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t
			\operatorname{E}_x\!\left[
			e^{-K^\alpha(u)}
			\Delta f\!\left(W^+_{\gamma^\alpha(u)}\right)
			\right]du
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t
			(S_u^\alpha\Delta f)(x)\,du.
		\end{align}
		This is \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-mild}. 
		
		By Step~1, the map
		\(u\mapsto S_u^\alpha(\Delta f)\) is continuous in \(C(\overline D)\).
		Hence, by the fundamental theorem of calculus applied to
		\eqref{eq:quenched-backward-mild},
		\[
		\frac{d}{dt}S_t^\alpha f
		=
		\frac12 S_t^\alpha(\Delta f).
		\]
		This completes the proof.

label: rem:quenched-no-semigroup
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:quenched-no-semigroup}
		Equation~\eqref{eq:quenched-backward-dynkin} holds for every
		$f\in C^2(\overline D)$, without imposing the boundary conditions
		defining $\mathcal D_\alpha$.
		The integral identity \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-mild}
		is established for $f\in\mathcal D_\alpha$.
		This class need not be dense in $C(\overline D)$.
		
		Indeed, if two visited regimes $i,j$ satisfy
		$\rho_i=\rho_j$ and $\kappa_i\neq\kappa_j$, then subtracting
		the two boundary conditions gives
		\[
		(\kappa_i-\kappa_j)f=0
		\qquad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		Thus every $f\in\mathcal D_\alpha$ vanishes on $\partial D$,
		and $\|1-f\|_\infty\ge1$.
		Hence $\mathcal D_\alpha$ is not dense in $C(\overline D)$
		in the uniform norm.
		
On the other hand,
\[
C_c^\infty(D)\subset\mathcal D_\alpha,
\]
so \(\mathcal D_\alpha\) is always nontrivial and infinite-dimensional.
Viewed as a class of functions on \(D\), it is dense in \(L^p(D,dx)\) for
every \(1\le p<\infty\), since \(C_c^\infty(D)\) is dense in these spaces.
This density is with respect to the interior Lebesgue measure only; it does
not extend to measures that charge the boundary \(\partial D\), which are
precisely the measures appearing in the forward formulation.
		
		We use \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-mild} as a test-function
		identity for the evolution defined by the stochastic
		representation.

title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Annealed sticky-elastic switching semigroup

title: Proof
body_md:
\medskip\noindent\emph{Step 1: contraction and semigroup property.}
		Both follow from Proposition~\ref{prop:operational-time-process}.
		
		
		\medskip
		\noindent\emph{Step 2: preservation of continuity.}
		Fix \(t>0\), \(i\in S\), and let \(x_m\to x\). Couple the reflected motions as in
		Lemma~\ref{lem:reflected-start-continuity}, using the same independent chain
		started from \(i\).
		
		As in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:quenched_sticky_elastic}, the reflected
		paths and local times converge uniformly in probability on bounded operational
		intervals. Since the chain has only finitely many jumps on such intervals, the
		corresponding clocks and killing functionals converge uniformly in probability,
		and so do their inverse clocks on compact physical-time intervals.
		
		It remains only to treat the chain evaluated at the inverse clock. For \(i\neq j\),
		let
		\[
		N_{ij}(s)
		:=
		\#\{u\le s:\alpha_{u-}=i,\ \alpha_u=j\}.
		\]
		Then the physical-time counting process \(N_{ij}(\gamma(t))\) has compensator
		\[
		\int_0^t q_{ij}\mathbf1_{\{I_{r-}=i\}}\,d\gamma(r).
		\]
		Since \(\gamma\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz, this compensator is absolutely continuous
		with respect to Lebesgue measure. Hence \(I\) has no jump at a fixed physical
		time. Therefore, almost surely, \(\gamma^x(t)\) is not a jump time of the common
		chain, and
		\[
		\alpha_{\gamma^{x_m}(t)}
		\longrightarrow
		\alpha_{\gamma^x(t)}
		\qquad\text{in probability}.
		\]
		
		Together with the convergences recalled above, this implies that the killed
		observables converge in probability. Since they are uniformly bounded by
		\(\|\Phi\|_\infty\), the convergence also holds in \(L^1\). Therefore
		\[
		(\mathcal S_t\Phi)(x_m,i)\to(\mathcal S_t\Phi)(x,i).
		\]
		
		\noindent\emph{Step 3: strong continuity.}
		Let
		\[
		q_*:=\max_{i\in S}(-q_{ii}).
		\]
		Because $\gamma(t)\le t$, the chain changes state before
		$\gamma(t)$ with probability at most $q_*t$. The reflected motion is
		uniformly stochastically continuous on the compact state space (recall the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:quenched_sticky_elastic}). Hence uniform
		continuity of $\Phi$ gives
		\[
		\sup_{(x,i)}
		\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
		\left|
		\Phi(W^+_{\gamma(t)},\alpha_{\gamma(t)})
		-\Phi(x,i)
		\right|
		\right]
		\longrightarrow0.
		\]
		The killing term satisfies
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_{x,i}[1-e^{-K(t)}]
		\le
		\|\kappa\|_\infty\operatorname{E}_x[L_t],
		\]
		which also tends to zero uniformly in $x$. Thus
		\[
		\|\mathcal S_t\Phi-\Phi\|_\infty\longrightarrow0,
		\qquad t\downarrow0.
		\]
		This proves strong continuity.
		
		\medskip
		\noindent\emph{Step 4: identification of the generator.}
		Let \(\Phi\in\mathcal D_0\), and set
		\[
		B(s):=\int_0^s\kappa(\alpha_u)\,dL_u.
		\]
		Applying the generalized It\^o formula for switching diffusions to
		\(\Phi(W_s^+,\alpha_s)\), together with the reflection term, gives
		\[
		d\Phi(W_s^+,\alpha_s)
		=
		d\mathcal M_s
		+
		(\mathcal L\Phi)_{\alpha_s}(W_s^+)\,ds
		-
		\partial_{\mathbf n}\Phi_{\alpha_s}(W_s^+)\,dL_s,
		\]
		where \(\mathcal M\) is a local martingale. Here the compensated jumps of
		\(\alpha\) produce the term
		\[
		\sum_{j\in S}q_{\alpha_s j}\Phi_j(W_s^+)\,ds
		\]
		appearing in \(\mathcal L\); see, e.g.,
		\cite[Section~2.2]{ngyuen2025_book}.
		
		Since
		\[
		d(e^{-B(s)})
		=
		-e^{-B(s)}\kappa(\alpha_s)\,dL_s,
		\]
		the product rule yields
		\begin{align}
			&e^{-B(\gamma(t))}
			\Phi(W^+_{\gamma(t)},\alpha_{\gamma(t)})
			-\Phi(x,i)
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			\mathcal N_t
			+
			\int_0^{\gamma(t)}
			e^{-B(s)}
			(\mathcal L\Phi)_{\alpha_s}(W_s^+)\,ds
			\nonumber\\
			&\quad
			-
			\int_0^{\gamma(t)}
			e^{-B(s)}
			\left(
			\partial_{\mathbf n}\Phi_{\alpha_s}
			+\kappa(\alpha_s)\Phi_{\alpha_s}
			\right)(W_s^+)\,dL_s,
			\label{eq:annealed-ito-formula}
		\end{align}
		where \(\mathcal N_t\) has zero expectation; indeed,
		\(\gamma(t)\le t\) is a bounded stopping time and all coefficients involved are
		bounded on \(\overline D\times S\).
		
		For \(\Phi\in\mathcal D_0\),
		\[
		-
		\left(
		\partial_{\mathbf n}\Phi_i+\kappa_i\Phi_i
		\right)
		=
		\rho_i(\mathcal L\Phi)_i
		\qquad\text{on }\partial D.
		\]
		Since \(dL_s\) is supported on \(\{W_s^+\in\partial D\}\), taking expectations
		in \eqref{eq:annealed-ito-formula} and using
		\[
		dA(s)=ds+\rho(\alpha_s)\,dL_s
		\]
		gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:annealed-dynkin-formula}
			(\mathcal S_t\Phi)(x,i)-\Phi(x,i)
			=
			\operatorname{E}_{x,i}\!\left[
			\int_0^{\gamma(t)}
			e^{-B(s)}
			(\mathcal L\Phi)_{\alpha_s}(W_s^+)\,dA(s)
			\right].
		\end{equation}
		
		Since \(A\) is continuous and strictly increasing, with inverse \(\gamma\),
		the change of variables \(r=A(s)\) gives
		\[
		\mathcal S_t\Phi-\Phi
		=
		\int_0^t\mathcal S_r(\mathcal L\Phi)\,dr.
		\]
		As \(\mathcal L\Phi\in C(\overline D\times S)\), strong continuity implies
		\[
		\left\|
		\frac{\mathcal S_t\Phi-\Phi}{t}-\mathcal L\Phi
		\right\|_\infty
		\le
		\sup_{0\le r\le t}
		\|\mathcal S_r(\mathcal L\Phi)-\mathcal L\Phi\|_\infty
		\longrightarrow0.
		\]
		Thus
		\[
		\Phi\in D(\mathcal G),
		\qquad
		\mathcal G\Phi=\mathcal L\Phi.
		\]
		
		\medskip
		\noindent\emph{Step 5: the backward equation.}
		The semigroup now gives the abstract Cauchy problem directly:
		$u(t)=\mathcal S_t\Phi$ is its unique mild solution.
		
		If $u$ is continuously differentiable in time with values in $C(\overline D\times S)$ and $u(t)\in\mathcal D_0$, the generator formula gives
		\eqref{eq:coupled-backward-system}, while membership in $\mathcal D_0$ gives
		\eqref{eq:coupled-sticky-elastic-bc}. The initial condition follows from
		strong continuity. Finally, substituting
		\[
		\partial_tu_i
		=
		\frac12\Delta u_i+\sum_{j\in S}q_{ij}u_j
		\]
		into \eqref{eq:coupled-sticky-elastic-bc} gives
		\eqref{eq:dynamic-wentzell-bc}.

body_md:
\label{rem:forward-density}
		The family \((\mu_t^\alpha)_{t\ge0}\) is the quenched spatial law associated
		with the frozen environment \(\alpha\).
		Equation~\eqref{eq:quenched-forward-dynkin} is its
		exact forward weak formulation. Equation~\eqref{eq:weak-forward-equation}
		is a closed relation only on the common test class
		\(\mathcal D_\alpha\).
		
		In general, without adjoining the operational phase as an additional state
		variable, one cannot expect a closed Markov forward equation or a uniqueness
		theorem based only on the spatial variable. This does not affect the
		homogenization result, which uses directly the quenched Feynman--Kac
		representation \eqref{eq:quenched-spatial-operator}.

label: cor:quenched-forward-homogenization
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:quenched-forward-homogenization}
		Let \(\mu_0\) be a finite nonnegative Radon measure on
		\(\overline D\). For every \(T>0\) and every \(0<\beta<1/8\), there
		exists \(C=C(T,\beta)>0\), independent of \(\varepsilon\) and
		\(\mu_0\), such that
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:forward-BL-fixed}
			\sup_{0\le t\le T}
			\operatorname{E}^\alpha
			\left[
			d_{\mathrm{BL}}
			\bigl(
			\mu_t^{\varepsilon,\alpha},
			\mu_t^0
			\bigr)
			\right]
			\le
			C\,\mu_0(\overline D)\,
			\varepsilon^\beta,
		\end{equation}
		and
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:forward-BL-uniform}
			\operatorname{E}^\alpha
			\left[
			\sup_{0\le t\le T}
			d_{\mathrm{BL}}
			\bigl(
			\mu_t^{\varepsilon,\alpha},
			\mu_t^0
			\bigr)
			\right]
			\le
			C\,\mu_0(\overline D)\,
			\varepsilon^\beta.
		\end{equation}
		In particular,
		\[
		\sup_{0\le t\le T}
		d_{\mathrm{BL}}
		\bigl(
		\mu_t^{\varepsilon,\alpha},
		\mu_t^0
		\bigr)
		\longrightarrow0
		\qquad
		\text{in }\operatorname{P}^\alpha\text{-probability}.
		\]
		Hence the quenched forward measures converge narrowly to the homogenized
		forward evolution, uniformly on bounded time intervals in probability.

			\right]

label: eq:Holder_bound_Wp
title: Proof
body_md:
\emph{Step 1: bound for \(W^{+}\).}
		We first prove that, for \(\theta<1/2\) and \(q\ge2\), there exists a
		constant \(C_{D,T,\theta,q}>0\), independent of the starting position \(x\),
		such that
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:Holder_bound_Wp}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D}
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[[W^+]_{\theta,T}^q\right]
			\le C_{D,T,\theta,q}<\infty.
		\end{equation}
		
		The reflected heat kernel satisfies the Gaussian bound
		\cite[Theorem~3.1 and Remark~3.11]{bass1991_some_potential_theory}:
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:neumann-heat-kernel-upper-bound}
			p^{W^+}(u,y,z)
			\le
			C^{(1)}_{D,T} u^{-d/2}
			\exp\left(
			-\frac{|z-y|^2}{C^{(2)}_D u}
			\right),
			\qquad
			0<u\le T,
			\quad y,z\in\overline D.
		\end{equation}
		
		The Markov property and
		\eqref{eq:neumann-heat-kernel-upper-bound} give, for
		\(0\le s<t\le T\) and \(a\ge2\),
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[
			|W_t^+-W_s^+|^a
			\right]
			&= \operatorname{E}_x\left[ \operatorname{E}  \left[{ 
				|W_t^+-W_s^+|^a \mid \mathcal F_{s} }\right] 
			\right]
			\\
			&=
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[
			\int_D
			|z-W_s^+|^a
			p^{W^+}(t-s,W_s^+,z)\,dz
			\right]
			\nonumber\\
			&\le
			C^{(1)}_{D,T}
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[
			\int_{\mathbb R^d}
			|\xi-W_s^+|^a
			(t-s)^{-d/2}
			\exp\left(
			-\frac{|\xi-W_s^+|^2}{C^{(2)}_D(t-s)}
			\right)\,d\xi
			\right]
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			C^{(1)}_{D,T}
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[
			\int_{\mathbb R^d}
			|\zeta|^a
			(t-s)^{-d/2}
			\exp\left(
			-\frac{|\zeta|^2}{C^{(2)}_D(t-s)}
			\right)\,d\zeta
			\right]
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			C^{(1)}_{D,T}
			\int_{\mathbb R^d}
			|\zeta|^a
			(t-s)^{-d/2}
			\exp\left(
			-\frac{|\zeta|^2}{C^{(2)}_D(t-s)}
			\right)\,d\zeta
			\nonumber\\
			&=
			C_{a,D,T}|t-s|^{a/2},
			\label{eq:reflected-bm-increment-moment}
		\end{align}
		where in the last step we used the change of variables
		\(\zeta=\sqrt{t-s}\,\eta\) and absorbed the resulting Gaussian moment
		into the constant \(C_{a,D,T}\).
		
		Choose now \(a>q\) so large that
		\[
		\theta < \frac12 - \frac1a.
		\]
		Kolmogorov's theorem in moment form
		\cite[Theorem~A.10]{friz2010_book}, with constants uniform in the starting
		point, gives
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x\left[[W^+]_{\theta,T}^q\right]
		\le C_{D,T,\theta,q}<\infty,
		\]
		which proves \eqref{eq:Holder_bound_Wp}.
		
		We turn to the regularity of the regulator \(L\).
		
		\emph{Step 2: smooth distance local time.}
		Let \(R_t=r(W_t^+)\). We first relate \(L\) to the right local time of \(R\).
		With our normalization,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:sloctime_limit}
			L_t = \lim_{\varepsilon \to 0} \frac{1}{2\varepsilon}
			\int_{0}^{t}
			\mathbf{1}_{\operatorname{dist}(W^+_s,\, \partial D)< \varepsilon} \,\mathrm{d} s. 
		\end{equation}
		The reflected SDE, with outward normal, is
		\cite{bass2005_uniqueness_for_reflecting}
		\begin{equation}
			\mathrm{d} W^+_t = \mathrm{d} W_t - \mathbf n(W^+_t) \,\mathrm{d} L_t,
		\end{equation}
		where \(W\) is a \(d\)-dimensional Brownian motion and \(\mathbf n\) is the
		outward unit normal vector on \(\partial D\).
		It\^o's formula gives
		\begin{align}
			\mathrm{d} R_t
			&= \nabla r(W^+_t) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W^+_t
			+ \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^{d}
			\partial_i \partial_j r(W^+_t)
			\,\mathrm{d} \langle (W^+)^i, (W^+)^j\rangle_t \\
			&= \nabla r(W^+_t) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W_t
			- \nabla r(W^+_t) \cdot \mathbf n(W^+_t) \,\mathrm{d} L_t
			+ \frac{1}{2} \Delta r(W^+_t) \,\mathrm{d} t,
		\end{align}
		where we used that the finite-variation reflection term does not contribute
		to quadratic variation, and hence
		\[
		\mathrm{d}\langle (W^+)^i,(W^+)^j\rangle_t
		=
		\delta_{ij}\,\mathrm{d} t.
		\]
		On the boundary, \(r\) is the inward distance, hence
		\[
		\nabla r(x) = -\mathbf n(x),
		\qquad
		\nabla r(x)\cdot \mathbf n(x) = -1.
		\]
		Since \(dL_t\) is supported on
		\(\{W^+_t\in\partial D\}=\{R_t=0\}\), we obtain
		\begin{equation}
			R_t = R_0
			+ \int_{0}^{t} \nabla r(W^+_u) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W_u
			+ L_t
			+ \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{t} \Delta r(W^+_u) \,\mathrm{d} u.
		\end{equation}
		Its quadratic variation is
		\begin{equation}
			\langle R \rangle_t
			=
			\sum_{i=1}^{d} \int_{0}^{t}
			 \left[{ \partial_{i} r(W^+_u) }\right] ^{2} \,\mathrm{d} u.
		\end{equation}
		
		Since \(R\ge0\), Tanaka's formula
		\cite[Theorem~VI.1.2]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales} gives
		\begin{equation}
			R_t - R_0
			=
			\int_{0}^{t} \mathbf{1}_{\{R_u>0\}} \,\mathrm{d} R_u
			+ \frac{1}{2} L^{0}_{t}(R),
		\end{equation}
		where \(L^{0}_{}(R)\) is the right local time of \(R\).
		Comparison with the preceding decomposition yields
		\begin{equation}
			\int_{0}^{t}
			\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u = 0\}} \nabla r(W^+_u) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W_u
			+ L_t
			+ \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{t}
			\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u = 0\}} \Delta r(W^+_u) \,\mathrm{d} u
			=
			\frac{1}{2} L^{0}_{t}(R).
		\end{equation}
		
		Since \(\partial D\) has zero Lebesgue measure and \(W_u^+\) admits a
		transition density for every \(u>0\),
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x\left[
		\int_0^T \mathbf{1}_{\{W_u^+\in\partial D\}}\,\,\mathrm{d} u
		\right]
		=
		\int_0^T
		\Pr_x(W_u^+\in\partial D)\,\,\mathrm{d} u
		=0.
		\]
		Hence
		\[
		\int_0^T \mathbf{1}_{\{R_u=0\}}\,\,\mathrm{d} u=0
		\qquad\text{a.s.}
		\]
		The boundary-supported martingale therefore has zero quadratic variation
		and hence vanishes
		\cite[Proposition~IV.1.13]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales}:
		\begin{equation}
			\left\langle
			\int_{0}^{\cdot}
			\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u = 0\}} \nabla r(W^+_u) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W_u
			\right\rangle_t
			=
			\int_0^t \mathbf{1}_{\{R_u=0\}}\,
			|\nabla r(W^+_u)|^2\,\,\mathrm{d} u
			=0.
		\end{equation}
		Likewise,
		\[
		\int_0^t \mathbf{1}_{\{R_u=0\}}\Delta r(W^+_u)\,\,\mathrm{d} u=0.
		\]
		Thus, with our normalization,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:loctime_relation}
			L_t=\frac12L^{0}_{t}(R).
		\end{equation}
		This factor \(1/2\) is precisely the convention fixed in
		Section~\ref{ssec:notation}; compare
		\cite[Section~VI.1]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales}.
		
		\medskip\noindent\emph{Step 3: bound for \(L\).}
		By Tanaka's formula applied to the nonnegative continuous semimartingale \(R\),
		and using the identity~\eqref{eq:loctime_relation}, for \(0\le s<t\le T\),
		\begin{align}
			L_t - L_s
			&=
			 \left({R_t - R_s}\right) 
			-
			\int_s^t \mathbf{1}_{\{R_u>0\}}\,\,\mathrm{d} R_u \\
			&=
			 \left({R_t - R_s}\right) 
			-
			 \left({M_t-M_s}\right) 
			-
			 \left({A_t-A_s}\right) ,
		\end{align}
		where
		\[
		M_t := \int_{0}^{t}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u > 0\}} \nabla r(W^+_u) \cdot \,\mathrm{d} W_u,
		\qquad
		A_t := \frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{t}
		\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u > 0\}} \Delta r(W^+_u) \,\mathrm{d} u.
		\]
		Here we used that \(dL_u\) is supported on \(\{R_u=0\}\), so the reflection
		term vanishes after multiplication by \(\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u>0\}}\).
		
		By convexity,
		\begin{equation}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|L_t - L_s|^{q}}\right] 
			\le
			3^{q-1}
			 \left({
				\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|R_t - R_s|^{q}}\right] 
				+ \operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|M_t - M_s|^{q}}\right] 
				+ \operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|A_t - A_s|^{q}}\right] 
			}\right) .
		\end{equation}
		
		Since \(r\) is Lipschitz on \(\overline D\),
		\begin{equation}
			|R_t - R_s|
			=
			|r(W^+_t) - r(W^+_s)|
			\le
			\mathrm{Lip}(r)\,|W^{+}_t - W^{+}_s|.
		\end{equation}
		Therefore, by Step~1,
		\begin{equation}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|R_t - R_s|^{q}}\right] 
			\le
			\mathrm{Lip}(r)^q C_{q,D,T} |t-s|^{q/2}.
		\end{equation}
		
		For the martingale term, BDG gives
		(see, e.g., \cite[Section~IV.4]{revuz1999Continuous_martingales})
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|M_t - M_s|^{q}}\right] 
			&\le C_{q}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{
				| \left\langle {M} \right\rangle _t -  \left\langle {M} \right\rangle _s|^{q/2}}\right]  \\
			&= C_{q} \operatorname{E}_x  \left[{
				 \left|{
					\int_{s}^{t}
					\mathbf{1}_{\{R_u > 0\}}
					|\nabla r(W^+_u)|^{2}
					\,\mathrm{d} u}\right|^{q/2}}\right]  \\
			&\le C_q  \left\|{\nabla r}\right\|_{\infty}^{q} |t-s|^{q/2}.
		\end{align}
		
		For the finite-variation term,
		\begin{align}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{|A_t - A_s|^{q}}\right] 
			&\le
			\frac{1}{2^q}
			 \left\|{\Delta r}\right\|_{\infty}^{q}
			|t-s|^{q} \\
			&\le
			\frac{1}{2^q}
			 \left\|{\Delta r}\right\|_{\infty}^{q}
			T^{q/2}
			|t-s|^{q/2}.
		\end{align}
		
		Combining the three bounds gives
		\begin{equation}
			\operatorname{E}_x  \left[{ |L_t - L_s|^{q} }\right] 
			\le
			C_{q,D,T}|t-s|^{q/2},
			\qquad 0\le s<t\le T.
		\end{equation}
		The same argument applies with \(q\) replaced by any \(a\ge2\). Hence
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:local-time-increment-moment}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D}
			\operatorname{E}_x \left[{|L_t-L_s|^a}\right] 
			\le
			C_{a,D,T}|t-s|^{a/2},
			\qquad 0\le s<t\le T.
		\end{equation}
		
		Now fix \(\theta<1/2\) and \(q\ge2\), and choose \(a>q\) large enough so that
		\[
		\theta < \frac12-\frac1a.
		\]
		Kolmogorov's theorem in moment form then gives
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\operatorname{E}_x\left[[L]_{\theta,T}^q\right]
		\le C_{D,T,\theta,q}<\infty.
		\]
		
		It remains to treat \(1\le q<2\). By Jensen's inequality,
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x[Z^q]
		=
		\operatorname{E}_x[(Z^2)^{q/2}]
		\le
		\operatorname{E}_x[Z^2]^{q/2}.
		\]
		Applying this with \(Z=[W^+]_{\theta,T}\) and
		\(Z=[L]_{\theta,T}\) extends the preceding \(q=2\) estimate to all
		\(1\le q<2\).
		This completes the proof.

body_md:
\label{lem:short-time-growth-local-time}
		Assume the notations of Section~\ref{ssec:notation}.
		Then, for every \(T>0\), there exists a constant
		\(C_{D,T}<\infty\) such that
		\begin{equation}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D}\operatorname{E}_x[L_t]
			\le C_{D,T} t^{1/2},
			\qquad 0<t\le T.
		\end{equation}
		Consequently, for every \(c>0\), there exists
		\(C_{D,T,c}<\infty\) such that, for every
		\(\varepsilon\in(0,1]\),
		\[
		\sup_{\xi\in\partial D}
		\operatorname{E}_\xi\left[
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\,dL_u
		\right]
		\le C_{D,T,c}\varepsilon^{1/2}.
		\]

label: eq:Revuz_formula_II
title: Proof
body_md:
Let \(p^{W^+}(t,x,y)\) be the reflected heat kernel. 
		With the Skorokhod-regulator normalization fixed in
		Section~\ref{ssec:notation}, the boundary local time
		\(L\) is the PCAF in Revuz correspondence with
		\(\frac12\sigma\); see, for example,
		\cite[Theorem~3.5]{Akhlil2012}.
		Therefore, for every nonnegative Borel
		function \(g\), the Revuz formula gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:Revuz_formula_II}
			\operatorname{E}_x\left[
			\int_0^t g(W_s^+)\,dL_s
			\right]
			=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t
			\int_{\partial D}
			g(\xi)\,
			p^{W^+}(s,x,\xi)\,
			d\sigma(\xi)\,ds ,
		\end{equation}
		see also \cite[proof of Theorem~5.3]{bass1991_some_potential_theory}. 
		Here, the heat kernel is taken with respect to Lebesgue measure, and \(\sigma\) denotes surface measure.
		
		Taking \(g\equiv1\) in \eqref{eq:Revuz_formula_II} gives
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:proof_Esp_ltime}
			\operatorname{E}_x[L_t]
			=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t\int_{\partial D}
			p^{W^+}(s,x,\xi)\,d\sigma(\xi)\,ds.
		\end{equation}
		
		The Gaussian heat-kernel bound
		\cite[Theorem~3.1 and Remark~3.11]{bass1991_some_potential_theory} gives, for every time-horizon \(T>0\),
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:proof_Gaussian_surface_bound}
			\int_{\partial D}p^{W^+}(s,x,\xi)\,d\sigma(\xi)
			\le
			C^{(1)}_{D,T}s^{-d/2}
			\int_{\partial D}
			\exp\left(-\frac{|x-\xi|^2}{C^{(2)}_{D}s}\right)\,d\sigma(\xi),
			\qquad 0<s\le T.
		\end{equation}
		The surface integral satisfies
		\[
		\sup_{x\in\overline D}
		\int_{\partial D}
		\exp\left(-\frac{|x-\xi|^2}{C^{(2)}_D s}\right)\,d\sigma(\xi)
		\le
		C_Ds^{(d-1)/2},
		\qquad s>0.
		\]
		Indeed, since \(\partial D\) is a compact \(C^2\) hypersurface, it admits a finite
		covering by \(C^1\) graph charts with uniformly bounded Jacobians. Hence, by
		the area formula,
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:surface_estimate}
			\sigma(\partial D\cap B(y,r))
			\le C_D r^{d-1},
			\qquad
			y\in\partial D,\quad 0<r\le r_0;
		\end{equation}
		see, e.g., \cite[\S 3.3.4.B]{evans2015measure}.
		If \(x\in\overline D\) and
		\(B(x,r)\cap\partial D\neq\emptyset\), choose
		\(y\in B(x,r)\cap\partial D\). Then
		\[
		B(x,r)\cap\partial D
		\subset B(y,2r)\cap\partial D.
		\]
		Thus \eqref{eq:surface_estimate} gives the same bound for
		\(x\in\overline D\) whenever \(2r\le r_0\). For larger \(r\), the bound
		follows after increasing \(C_D\), since \(\sigma(\partial D)<\infty\).
		Hence
		\[
		\sigma(\partial D\cap B(x,r))
		\le C_Dr^{d-1},
		\qquad x\in\overline D,\quad r>0.
		\]
		
		We decompose \(\partial D\) into the disjoint dyadic annuli 
		\[
		A_0:=\partial D\cap B(x,2\sqrt{s}),\qquad
		A_n:=\partial D\cap
		\bigl(B(x,2^{n+1}\sqrt{s})\setminus B(x,2^n\sqrt{s})\bigr),
		\quad n\ge1.
		\]
		Then
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\int_{\partial D}
			\exp\left(-\frac{|x-\xi|^2}{C^{(2)}_D s}\right)\,d\sigma(\xi)
			&\le
			\sigma(A_0)
			+
			\sum_{n\ge1}
			\exp\left(-\frac{2^{2n}}{C^{(2)}_D}\right)\sigma(A_n)\\
			&\le
			C_Ds^{(d-1)/2}
			+
			C_Ds^{(d-1)/2}
			\sum_{n\ge1}
			2^{(n+1)(d-1)}
			\exp\left(-\frac{2^{2n}}{C^{(2)}_D}\right)\\
			&\le
			C_Ds^{(d-1)/2}.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		Substituting this into~\eqref{eq:proof_Gaussian_surface_bound} yields
		\begin{equation}
			\label{eq:boundary-kernel-integral}
			\sup_{x\in\overline D}
			\int_{\partial D}p^{W^+}(s,x,\xi)\,d\sigma(\xi)
			\le
			\widetilde C_{D,T}s^{-1/2},
			\qquad 0<s\le T.
		\end{equation}
		By~\eqref{eq:proof_Esp_ltime} and
		\eqref{eq:boundary-kernel-integral},
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_x[L_t]
		\le
		\frac{\widetilde C_{D,T}}{2}
		\int_0^t s^{-1/2}\,ds
		=
		\widetilde C_{D,T}t^{1/2},
		\qquad 0<t\le T.
		\]
		This proves the first estimate. 
		
		For the discounted bound, use the same Revuz
		formula with weight \(e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\):
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_\xi\left[
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\,dL_u
		\right]
		=
		\frac12
		\int_0^T
		e^{-cu/\varepsilon}
		\int_{\partial D}p^{W^+}(u,\xi,\eta)\,d\sigma(\eta)\,du.
		\]
		Therefore, by \eqref{eq:boundary-kernel-integral},
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_\xi\left[
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\,dL_u
		\right]
		\le
		\frac{\widetilde C_{D,T}}2
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}u^{-1/2}\,du.
		\]
		By the change of variables \(v=cu/\varepsilon\),
		\[
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}u^{-1/2}\,du
		=
		\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{c}\right)^{1/2}
		\int_0^{cT/\varepsilon} e^{-v}v^{-1/2}\,dv
		\le
		\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{c}\right)^{1/2}
		\int_0^\infty e^{-v}v^{-1/2}\,dv.
		\]
		Since
		\[
		\int_0^\infty e^{-v}v^{-1/2}\,dv
		=
		\Gamma(1/2)<\infty,
		\]
		setting
		\[
		C_{D,T,c}
		:=
		\frac{\widetilde C_{D,T}}2\,
		c^{-1/2}\Gamma(1/2),
		\]
		we obtain
		\[
		\operatorname{E}_\xi\left[
		\int_0^T e^{-cu/\varepsilon}\,dL_u
		\right]
		\le
		C_{D,T,c}\varepsilon^{1/2}.
		\]
		The estimate is uniform in \(\xi\).
		This completes the proof.

body_md:
Since \(S_t^\alpha\) is a contraction on \(C(\overline D)\), duality gives
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\|\mu_t^\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}
			&=
			\sup_{\substack{f\in C(\overline D)\\ \|f\|_\infty\le1}}
			\left|
			\int_{\overline D}f\,d\mu_t^\alpha
			\right|
			\\
			&=
			\sup_{\substack{f\in C(\overline D)\\ \|f\|_\infty\le1}}
			\left|
			\int_{\overline D}S_t^\alpha f\,d\mu_0
			\right|
			\\
			&\le
			\|\mu_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}},
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		where the first identity is the norm characterization in the
		Riesz--Markov--Kakutani theorem; see, e.g.,
		\cite[Theorem~6.19]{rudin1987real}.
		If \(\kappa\equiv0\), then \(S_t^\alpha1=1\), and therefore
		\[
		\mu_t^\alpha(\overline D)
		=
		\mu_0(\overline D).
		\]
		
		
		For every $f\in C(\overline D)$ and every fixed $x$,
		continuity of the time-changed spatial path and of the killing
		functional, together with bounded convergence, gives
		$S_t^\alpha f(x)\to S_s^\alpha f(x)$ as $t\to s$.
		Since $|S_t^\alpha f(x)|\le\|f\|_\infty$, dominated convergence
		with respect to the finite measure $|\mu_0|$ yields
		\[
		\int_{\overline D} f\,d\mu_t^\alpha
		=
		\int_{\overline D}S_t^\alpha f\,d\mu_0
		\longrightarrow
		\int_{\overline D}S_s^\alpha f\,d\mu_0
		=
		\int_{\overline D}f\,d\mu_s^\alpha.
		\]
		This proves narrow continuity.
		
		
		Integrating \eqref{eq:quenched-backward-dynkin} with respect to
		\(\mu_0(dx)\) gives \eqref{eq:quenched-forward-dynkin}.
		
		If \(f\in\mathcal D_\alpha\), then
		\eqref{eq:quenched-backward-mild} gives
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			\int_{\overline D}f\,d\mu_t^\alpha
			-
			\int_{\overline D}f\,d\mu_0
			&=
			\int_{\overline D}
			(S_t^\alpha f-f)\,d\mu_0
			\\
			&=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t
			\int_{\overline D}
			S_s^\alpha(\Delta f)(x)\,\mu_0(dx)\,ds
			\\
			&=
			\frac12
			\int_0^t
			\int_{\overline D}
			\Delta f(y)\,\mu_s^\alpha(dy)\,ds.
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		This proves \eqref{eq:weak-forward-equation} and
		\eqref{eq:weak-forward-derivative}. 
		
		For \eqref{eq:weak-forward-time-dependent}, fix $\varphi$ as in the statement
		and set $g(t):=\int_{\overline D}\varphi(t,x)\,\mu_t^\alpha(dx)$. Writing, for
		$h>0$,
		\[
		\frac{g(t+h)-g(t)}{h}
		=
		\int_{\overline D}\frac{\varphi(t+h,\cdot)-\varphi(t,\cdot)}{h}\,d\mu_{t+h}^\alpha
		+
		\frac{1}{h}\left(
		\int_{\overline D}\varphi(t,\cdot)\,d\mu_{t+h}^\alpha
		-
		\int_{\overline D}\varphi(t,\cdot)\,d\mu_t^\alpha
		\right),
		\]
		the first term converges to $\int_{\overline D}\partial_t\varphi(t,\cdot)\,d\mu_t^\alpha$
		by $\varphi\in C^1([0,T];C(\overline D))$, the uniform boundedness
		$\|\mu_t^\alpha\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\|\mu_0\|_{\mathrm{TV}}$, and narrow
		continuity; the second term converges to
		$\tfrac12\int_{\overline D}\Delta\varphi(t,\cdot)\,d\mu_t^\alpha$ by
		\eqref{eq:weak-forward-derivative}, since $\varphi(t,\cdot)\in\mathcal D_\alpha$.
		Hence $g$ is continuously differentiable with
		$g'(t)=\int_{\overline D}(\partial_t\varphi+\tfrac12\Delta\varphi)\,d\mu_t^\alpha$,
		and integrating from $0$ to $T$ gives \eqref{eq:weak-forward-time-dependent}.
